title: AI governance without an AI team: A practical escalation framework for businesses
summary: Build an AI governance framework with approved tools, clear guardrails and escalation steps for your business.
body_markdown:
Artificial intelligence in business is increasingly being used across organizations, from drafting content and supporting customers to analyzing data and streamlining everyday tasks. According to the[U.S. Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS)](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2026/05/ai-use-businesses.html) , 17 percent to 20 percent of businesses used AI between December 2025 and May 2026, with 20 percent to 23 percent expecting to use it in the following six months.


AI’s versatility has fueled rapid adoption, but it also raises the stakes. The more employees use AI tools, the more important clear guidelines become. Without an artificial intelligence framework, businesses risk exposing sensitive information, relying on inaccurate outputs or even allowing AI to make decisions without appropriate oversight.


The good news is that small to medium-sized businesses don't need a dedicated AI team to manage these risks. With a practical AI framework, you can establish clear rules that help your employees use AI confidently and responsibly.


## Why AI governance matters


So what exactly is an AI governance framework? AI governance refers to the policies, responsibilities and safeguards that guide how a business uses AI. A framework helps employees understand what's acceptable, where human oversight is required and how to respond when something goes wrong.


The challenge is that[AI adoption in the workplace](https://www.ooma.com/blog/business/states-fastest-to-adopt-ai-in-workplace/) has outpaced the development of such frameworks. IBM's 2025[Cost of a Data Breach Report](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2025-07-30-ibm-report-13-of-organizations-reported-breaches-of-ai-models-or-applications,-97-of-which-reported-lacking-proper-ai-access-controls) found that 97 percent of organizations that reported breaches of AI models or applications lacked proper AI access controls. Moreover, 63 percent of organizations surveyed had no AI governance policy or were still developing one, and among organizations with policies in place, only 34 percent regularly audited for unsanctioned AI use.


Without clear rules and ongoing oversight, the consequences of using AI in the workplace can go beyond a single bad output:


- **Ethical dilemmas:** Models can reflect biases in their training data, leading to unfair treatment in areas like hiring or customer service.
- **Regulatory penalties:** Rules like the EU AI Act and GDPR carry steep fines for non-compliance, including misuse of personal data and prohibited AI practices.
- **Privacy and data exposure:** Employees could enter private or proprietary information into AI tools that store prompts and responses or even use them to train their models, depending on the provider’s policies and settings. Shared conversation histories, overly broad access permissions or security breaches can also expose sensitive information to others.
- **Poor decisions:** AI can produce confident but inaccurate or outdated answers. Those errors can then quietly shape high-stakes decisions, from product strategy to budgeting, with repercussions that are costly to reverse.
- **Loss of consumer trust:** A single data leak, biased decision or AI-generated mistake can damage a brand's reputation.


The goal of AI governance then is to mitigate those risks by helping teams understand where AI tools can add value, where caution is needed and how to respond when things go wrong.


## Building a practical AI framework


Effective AI risk management can begin with four practical steps that help employees understand how to use the technology.


### 1. Define which AI tools and tasks are approved


Start by identifying which business AI tools employees can use and for what purposes. Create a list of approved tools and common use cases, such as brainstorming, drafting internal documents or summarizing nonconfidential information.


You can also highlight what's off-limits, such as providing a list of explicitly unapproved tools or tasks that shouldn’t be touched by AI.


### 2. Set simple AI guardrails for everyday work


Once you've defined approved tools and tasks, establish a few rules for *how* employees should use AI for work. This can include guidelines on which types of information are okay to feed into LLMs or how many layers of human review are needed.


For instance, while employees should always verify AI-generated facts, calculations and recommendations before relying on them, customer-facing content or higher-stakes analyses may require additional review by someone with the appropriate expertise.


Try to keep these[AI tips](https://www.ooma.com/blog/useful-ai-tips-and-tools-for-small-businesses/) and guardrails easy to understand and apply. A short set of practical rules is more useful than a lengthy policy employees struggle to interpret.


### 3. Assign clear ownership


While you may not need a dedicated AI team overseeing operations, you should still assign certain AI responsibilities to those who understand your business operations, technology and risks.


For example, the IT team could be responsible for the approved-tool list, while legal or compliance teams could be the point for data concerns or regulatory questions. Similarly, department managers could own how AI can be used by their teams.


The idea is to make it easy for employees to know who to contact for approvals, exceptions and concerns. Be sure to also review responsibilities periodically as your business adopts new tools or expands its use of AI.


### 4. Establish a clear escalation process


Even with clear rules, employees will likely encounter situations that don’t fit neatly. This is where a clear escalation protocol can help them respond consistently.


A simple way to put this into practice is a three-action framework. Before using AI for a task, employees ask which of these applies:


- **Proceed:** The task falls under approved independent use. Typically, this means an approved tool, low-risk work and no sensitive information. Employees can move forward, checking the output before they use it.
- **Pause and review:** The task involves sensitive data, claims that will be publicly published or major decisions that affect others. Employees get sign-off from a manager or the designated AI point person before moving forward.
- **Stop and escalate:** Something has gone wrong, such as sensitive information being exposed or an automated system taking an unexpected action. Employees halt the workflow and report it to the designated AI point person or team immediately.


With AI still in its early stages, new and unexpected challenges are bound to emerge. Make it clear that early reporting is expected and welcomed so your business can investigate and respond promptly without anyone fearing blame.


## Make responsible AI use part of everyday work


As AI for companies becomes more embedded in daily operations and documented AI incidents continue[to rise](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/responsible-ai) , strong governance is essential to[keep AI automation from going too far](https://www.ooma.com/blog/business/human-handoff-problem-in-ai-customer-service/) .


For small to medium businesses, several well-defined processes can give your organization a foundation for adopting new tools while protecting your employees, customers and company interests.


With the right foundations in place, you can then further leverage AI to make everyday operations more efficient.
